preamble.summary: LXX Hosea is among the most frequently quoted Minor Prophets in the NT. Four of Hosea's key sayings shape foundational New Testament theology in their LXX form: the covenant-inclusion formula at 2:23, the 'mercy not sacrifice' of 6:6, 'out of Egypt I called my son' at 11:1, and the death-taunt at 13:14. The LXX of Hosea is sometimes difficult in Hebrew and the translators struggled with obscure idioms, but the NT-quoted passages all render cleanly.
preamble.notable_variants: The 2:23 'not my people / my people' formula quoted at Romans 9:25 and 1 Peter 2:10 as the ground for Gentile inclusion; the 6:6 mercy-not-sacrifice saying quoted twice by Jesus in Matthew (9:13, 12:7); the 11:1 'out of Egypt I called my son' that Matthew 2:15 applies to Jesus' return from Egypt; the death-taunt of 13:14 quoted triumphantly at 1 Corinthians 15:54–55.
preamble.theological_legacy: These four LXX Hosea passages are among the densest knots of LXX-dependent NT theology anywhere in the Minor Prophets. Gentile inclusion, mercy over sacrifice, Christological exile-typology, and resurrection triumph — all are argued in the NT using LXX Hosea's specific Greek wording.

renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ ἐρῶ τῷ οὐ λαῷ μου λαός μου εἶ σύ
renderings.mt_rendering: I will say to 'Not My People,' 'You are my people'
renderings.lxx_rendering: I will say to 'Not My People,' 'You are my people'
notes: Romans 9:25 quotes this verse verbatim in its LXX form as proof that God has called 'not my people' to become his people: 'Those who were not my people I will call my people, and her who was not beloved I will call beloved.' Paul's argument for Gentile inclusion runs directly through LXX Hosea.

1 Peter 2:10 ('Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy') reworks the same Hosea passage into an explicitly Gentile-Christian ecclesiology.
Two independent NT books deploy LXX Hosea 2:23 for the same theological move — this is one of the clearest cases of shared early-Christian exegesis built on the Greek OT.

renderings.lxx_reading: διότι ἔλεος θέλω καὶ οὐ θυσίαν
renderings.mt_rendering: For I desire faithful love and not sacrifice
renderings.lxx_rendering: For I desire mercy and not sacrifice
notes: Jesus quotes this verse twice in Matthew's Gospel: at 9:13 (defending his table-fellowship with tax collectors and sinners) and at 12:7 (defending his disciples' Sabbath grain-picking). Both citations use the LXX's wording — eleos thelō kai ou thysian — verbatim.

Hebrew chesed ('faithful love, covenant loyalty') is rendered eleos ('mercy'), the standard LXX equivalence. Jesus' weaponizing of this LXX verse against legal formalism is quintessentially Matthean: the Greek text serves as an authoritative Scriptural voice against ritual observance divorced from compassion.
This is one of only a handful of OT verses that Jesus is remembered as quoting twice, in both cases to settle a halakhic dispute in favor of mercy.

renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ ἐξ Αἰγύπτου μετεκάλεσα τὰ τέκνα αὐτοῦ
renderings.mt_rendering: out of Egypt I called my son
renderings.lxx_rendering: and out of Egypt I recalled his children
notes: Matthew 2:15 cites Hosea 11:1 as fulfilled in Jesus' return from Egypt: 'Out of Egypt I called my son.' Matthew's Greek — ex Aigyptou ekalesa ton huion mou — does NOT follow the standard LXX (which has the plural 'children' and the verb metekalesa), but aligns more closely with the Hebrew and with Aquila's Greek revision.

This is one of the clearest cases where Matthew follows a Greek OT text that is not the standard Rahlfs LXX — evidence that Matthew's OT was not the Septuagint we have but a related, more literal Greek tradition (what scholars call 'kaige-Theodotion' or a proto-Aquila revision).
The passage underscores that 'the Septuagint' in the first century was a diverse family of Greek Bibles, not a single edition.

renderings.mt_reading: אֱהִי דְבָרֶיךָ מָוֶת אֱהִי קָטָבְךָ שְׁאוֹל
renderings.lxx_reading: ποῦ ἡ δίκη σου θάνατε ποῦ τὸ κέντρον σου ᾅδη
renderings.mt_rendering: Where are your plagues, O Death? Where is your destruction, O Sheol?
renderings.lxx_rendering: Where is your penalty, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades?
notes: 1 Corinthians 15:55 quotes this verse in resurrection-triumph mode: 'O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?' Paul's wording — pou sou thanate to nikos, pou sou thanate to kentron — modifies the LXX's pou to kentron sou hadē to pou sou thanate to kentron (fusing Hades and Death into one addressee).

The LXX's kentron ('sting, goad') is the specific Greek word Paul uses. The whole 1 Corinthians 15:55 pericope is Paul's reworking of LXX Hosea 13:14 combined with LXX Isaiah 25:8 (katepien ho thanatos ischysas, 'death has been swallowed up in victory').

This conflated citation is one of the most elaborate pieces of LXX-dependent NT composition. The whole climactic crescendo of 1 Corinthians 15 hangs on the specific Greek verbs the LXX chose for Isaiah 25 and Hosea 13.
